goal: The developers build a product with which its users achieve their goals.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers know whom the product serves and what each of them is trying to achieve.
The developers can tell whether a change brings the users closer to their goals.
The developers know what sets the product apart from the way users work today.

necessary_conditions.what: Does Roles list every kind of person who comes to the product with a goal of their own?
Does each objective state, in one sentence, what one role is trying to achieve in their own work?
Does the vision describe only what the users do and get, not how the product works inside?
Does each objective have key results that measure how well and how fast its role achieves it, each with the direction that's better?
Are the objectives distinct, so that each piece of work serves one of them?
Does the concept name the users' current way of working and the few ideas that set the product apart from it, the first being what the product values most?

practices.thinking: The developers build for the people Roles lists, so a missing role goes unserved, and two roles merged into one get a product that fits neither. Define each role by the job it hires the product to do, as in Clayton Christensen's theory of the jobs that customers hire a product for, not by a job title. Start from the job that the product exists to do, and name who hires it for that job. Then ask whether that job gets done only if the product also does a job for someone else, such as setting it up on a shared server. Each such person is a role as well. Split a role whose members hire the product for different jobs. Name the role `user` where there's only one. Check that each role has a job that no other role has.

steps.text: Ask the user about each person whose job you can't tell from what the product does.

practices.thinking: The developers build toward the objectives, so each must name the end that a role reaches. A feature or a measure of that end isn't an objective. An objective in John Doerr's Measure What Matters is a qualitative goal that a key result then measures. For each role, write its job as the end they reach in their own work, in one sentence with the role as the subject. Ask why that end matters to them until the answer is their own goal and no longer the product's. Write one objective for each distinct end. Check that the objective still makes sense with the product's name taken out.

The vision must stay true while the inside of the product changes, so it describes only the problem space: what users do and get. How the product does it belongs to the solution space, in the architecture. For each sentence, ask whether it would change if the product's internals changed while users saw the same. If it would, move it to the architecture.

The developers keep a change only if it brings the users closer to their goals, so each objective needs measures that show that after a change. The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standard 9241-11 defines usability by effectiveness and efficiency, among other measures, and these give the two key results. The first measures how well: the share of attempts in which the role reaches the objective, or its complement, such as the share of deliverables the users can't use. The second measures how fast: the time or effort the role spends to reach it. Give each the direction that's better. Rank them: keep a change that improves one only if none ranked before it gets worse, with how well before how fast. Give no targets, since a measure made a target stops being a good measure, as Goodhart's law says. Check that a developer can measure both after a change and decide from them whether to keep it.

The developers decide what to build by asking which objective a piece of work serves, which works only if the objectives don't overlap. For each pair of objectives, ask whether a piece of work could serve one without the other. If not, merge them. Then take the work the product plans, and name the objective each piece serves. A piece that serves none is either not needed or shows a missing objective. Ask the user which.

The developers make many choices that no line of the vision names, and the concept lets each of them lean the same way. April Dunford's positioning method, in Obviously Awesome, gives the decisions in order. First, name the current way: what the users do today without the product, such as asking an AI in one prompt and fixing its draft. Second, for each key result, ask what in the current way makes the role fall short on it, and name the cause. Third, for each cause that the product removes, write the idea by which it removes it, and what that gives the role toward the objective. Put first the idea that moves the first key result most, so that it settles a choice where the others conflict. Check that, given a design choice no line names, a developer can decide it by the first idea.

steps.text: Ask the user which idea the product values most, if the objectives don't settle it.
